stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing Barron's Premium 2027 Chapter 3, Topic 1.5, 'Resistance to Slavery and the Development of Maroon Communities.'
stimulus.text: As Africans were brought into the slavery system, they developed forms of cultural resistance that tried, against great odds, to preserve traditional patterns and a sense of autonomy. One notable form was the Maroon community: enslaved Africans who escaped and built independent settlements. These communities existed throughout the New World, many in the Caribbean and Brazil. Often they were formed by first-generation Africans, who carried memories of Africa with them. Their traditions included medicinal herbs, drumming, and dancing as part of healing rituals. One of the largest Maroon communities was Palmares in Brazil, established in the early 1600s, with more than 30,000 residents, which held out until the Portuguese conquered it in 1694.

stem: The passage says Maroons preserved African traditions, including medicinal herbs, drumming, and dancing as part of healing rituals. A historian studying African cultural survival in the Americas would find this evidence most useful for which purpose?

options.text: Proving that all enslaved Africans kept identical traditions everywhere.
Showing how first-generation Africans carried traditions into the Americas and passed them on.
Showing that Maroons had no contact at all with European culture or religion.
Proving that African traditions disappeared entirely within a single generation.

instruction: Pick one option from the stimulus and stem only. Do not open the question file.
